title: -nál/-nél at the Gate, -on/-re at the Airport

sections.title: Two different nouns, two different case families
sections.content: kapu ("gate") behaves like ajtó ("door") — a small, point-like spot you stand AT — so it takes the -nál/-nél family: a kapunál vagyok ("I'm at the gate"), a kapuhoz megyek ("I'm going to the gate"). repülőtér itself behaves differently: like pályaudvar, it takes the -on/-en/-ön family instead — a repülőtéren vagyok ("I'm at the airport"), a repülőtérre megyek ("I'm going to the airport"). Two nouns, two families — there's no way to predict which from the word alone, so it's worth learning repülőtér's pattern as a fixed pair with pályaudvar's.

sections.title: Two case families side by side
rows: at the gate / to the gate
at the airport / to the airport
at the station / to the station

items.spanish: Hol vagy? A hetes kapunál vagyok.
items.english: Where are you? I'm at gate seven.
We're going to the airport now.

sections.content: When in doubt, picture the place: a gate or a desk is a specific point you stand next to (-nál/-nél), while a whole building like the airport or the station is a place you're on the grounds of (-on/-en/-ön) — the same feel as a téren, "on the square".
